# Job Chapter 2 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 416v

---

**1** On another day the heavenly beings came to present themselves before the LORD, and the Accuser came with them. **2** "Where have you come from?" the LORD asked the Accuser. "From patrolling the earth," he replied, "roaming back and forth across it."

**3** Then the LORD said to the Accuser, "Have you noticed my servant Job? There is no one on earth like him — a man of complete integrity, who fears God and stays far from evil. And he still maintains his integrity, even though you persuaded me to ruin him for no reason." **4** "Skin for skin!" the Accuser replied. "A man will give everything he has to save his own life. **5** But reach out and strike his flesh and bones, and he will certainly curse you to your face."

**6** "Very well," the LORD said to the Accuser. "He is in your power. But you must spare his life."

**7** So the Accuser left the LORD's presence and afflicted Job with terrible boils from head to foot. **8** Job sat among the ashes, scraping his sores with a piece of broken pottery.

**9** His wife said to him, "Are you still trying to hold on to your integrity? Curse God and be done with it — die!" **10** But Job replied, "You are talking like a foolish woman. Should we accept only good things from God and never anything bad?" In all this, Job did not sin with his lips.

**11** When three of Job's friends heard about all the disasters that had struck him, they set out from their homes — Eliphaz from Teman, Bildad from Shuah, and Zophar from Naamah. They met together and traveled to Job to sympathize with him and comfort him. **12** When they saw him from a distance, they could barely recognize him. They broke down weeping, tore their robes, and threw dust into the air over their heads. **13** Then they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, because they could see how terrible his suffering was.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**"You persuaded me to ruin him for no reason":** This is one of the most theologically loaded lines in the Hebrew Bible. God admits to the Accuser — and to the reader — that Job's suffering serves no moral purpose. It undermines the entire retribution theology that Job's friends will spend the next thirty chapters defending.

**Job's wife:** She is often vilified, but her words deserve a more sympathetic reading. She has lost everything Job has lost — all ten children, all their wealth. Her counsel may be born of compassion: if God has abandoned you, why prolong the agony? She is the only person in the book who speaks to Job out of shared grief rather than theology.

**Seven days of silence:** The most compassionate thing the friends do in the entire book happens before they open their mouths. Once they begin speaking, they will become instruments of additional suffering.

---
*— PNEUMA*
